extraction.research_question: (1) What are the characteristics of access to grocery stores for different sub-populations at different stages of disasters? (2) What is the extent of disparity in access among different sociodemographic groups in different disaster phases? (3) What are the contributing factors to unequal access to grocery stores, and to what extent are facility distribution inequities, such as food deserts, indicative of access disparities? (p.2, lines 106-112)
extraction.theory: Access to facilities is treated as three complementary dimensions: redundancy (number of distinct stores visited), rapidity (trip duration, reflecting traffic and road disruption and restoration of system function), and proximity (trip distance). The paper argues that physical-distance and food-desert measures are inadequate in disasters because disruption changes store availability and trip time, and because household capabilities and protective behavior shape access. Framing draws on accessibility and resilience literature (refs 6, 22-28, 33-35). It is not a formal behavioral or economic theory.
extraction.data: Unit of analysis: census-tract-aggregated traffic analysis zones (TAZs) as population nodes, linked to grocery points-of-interest (POIs) as facility nodes. Sample: 1,804 TAZs, 920 grocery stores, 6,052 TAZ-POI links in Harris County, Texas (Fig. 2a caption, p.4). Period: StreetLight O-D trips for 1 Aug to 30 Sep 2017. Analysis window 1 Aug to 15 Sep 2017 (p.6). Baseline 1-20 Aug 2017 (weekday-matched). Normal-period clustering window is stated as 5-16 Aug in the text and 7-16 Aug in the Fig. 3 caption, so it is inconsistent. Sources: StreetLight Data (anonymized cell and GPS trips, not individual-level counts reported; the paper cites more than 40 billion records nationally per month); SafeGraph POIs (grocery, specialty food and general merchandise categories, manually filtered); ACS 2015-2019 5-year estimates; FEMA Harvey flood depth grid; USDA Food Access Research Atlas. The StreetLight penetration rate is given as "approximately 23 penetration rate" in the extracted text, which appears garbled and should be verified in the PDF. Data access is restricted by license and code is available on request.
extraction.method:
Descriptive population-facility network analysis plus unsupervised time-series clustering. (1) Build directed bipartite TAZ-to-POI networks (unweighted; weighted by trip duration; weighted by trip distance) from daily aggregated trips (Table 1, Eqs. 1-3). (2) Compute three TAZ-level indicators: unweighted degree (unique POIs visited), average weighted degree for duration (seconds), and average weighted degree for distance (miles). (3) Express each indicator as percentage change from the weekday baseline, Pc = (M - B)/B (Eq. 4, p.5). (4) Impute gaps with a Kalman filter via R imputeTS after dropping TAZs with 5+ consecutive missing days. (5) Smooth with a 3-day moving average, then run partitional multivariate DTW clustering (dtwclust, R). Cluster number is chosen with COP and modified Davies-Bouldin indices, and the chosen k and the cluster sizes are not reported in the text. (6) Compare sociodemographic and facility characteristics across clusters and income groups (ANOVA, Tukey, chi-square, a two-sample proportion test, and a correlation between number of POIs in a TAZ and each percentage change). Phases: normal (pre-event), preparation (single focal day 24 Aug 2017, the largest percentage change, before landfall on 25 Aug), and impact/short-term recovery (flood-affected TAZs). Flooded TAZ = flood extent above 6.5% of TAZ area (the 75th percentile in Harris County).</method>
<parameter name="identification">None. The study is descriptive and associational. Group comparisons (income tertiles, food-desert status, clusters) and phase comparisons are not causal. The paper uses causal language in places ("disproportionately exacerbated", "flooding disproportionally affects"), which the design does not support. The text mentions a "multivariate analysis" (p.13) but no model, coefficients or specification are reported.
extraction.scope: Population: residents of Harris County, Texas (Houston metro), identified by home TAZ, who visited grocery stores in August-September 2017. Institutions: grocery stores and supermarkets (including warehouse clubs, supercenters and eating places in the category filter). Era: a single event, Hurricane Harvey (landfall 25 Aug 2017, over 60 inches of rain). Single county, single storm, single month window. The paper's own claim about generalizing beyond this event is not present.

key_findings.finding: Normal-period clusters on the three access indicators show spatial clustering, and the three sets of clusters barely overlap. Areas with low redundancy are concentrated in the east and south of the county, and large northern TAZs have poor proximity and rapidity.
key_findings.numbers: Three clusters per indicator; Fig. 3d shows group counts in parentheses, which are not extracted in the text.

key_findings.finding: The normal-period cluster with the highest redundancy is described as lower socioeconomic status. This conflicts with the Table 3 values as extracted (see limitations).
key_findings.numbers: Table 3 extracted: per-capita income for the highest-redundancy cluster C1 = $36,008.19 (starred, significant) vs $28,305.49 and $28,305.94; food-desert share 0.45* vs 0.38 and 0.34; stores per TAZ 0.67 vs 1.03 and 1.87*.

key_findings.finding: Preparation phase (24 Aug 2017): high-income TAZs had a significantly larger increase in unique stores visited than low-income TAZs (ANOVA and Tukey, alpha 0.05). Lower-income TAZs with long normal-period trips had a disproportionately larger increase in trip duration. High-income TAZs with short normal-period distances had the largest increase in distance.
key_findings.numbers: No effect sizes, means or test statistics for these comparisons appear in the text, only boxplots.

key_findings.finding: Correlation between number of POIs in a TAZ and each percentage change in access indicators during preparation is very weak. The text reads it as a slight association for redundancy only, and no association for duration or distance.
key_findings.numbers: Visited-POI % change r = -0.06, p = 0.007; duration % change r = -0.01, p = 0.448; distance % change r = -0.03, p = 0.100.

key_findings.finding: Within food deserts, high-income TAZs visited more POIs during preparation without significantly longer trips or distances than low-income TAZs in food deserts. The authors conclude food-desert status alone does not capture preparation access.
key_findings.location: Results, income x food desert, pp.9-10 (lines 630-657; Fig. 5)
key_findings.numbers: No counts or test statistics for the four income x food-desert groups in the text.

key_findings.finding: Among flood-affected TAZs during impact and short-term recovery, two access clusters emerge. Cluster 2 shows a larger increase in unique POIs visited and a smaller loss of proximity and rapidity. Cluster 2 has higher income, a lower minority share, a higher chance of food-desert status, and fewer POIs per TAZ.
key_findings.numbers: Two clusters; cluster sizes not reported in the text.

key_findings.finding: Income and food-desert status interact in the recovery clusters. Among cluster 2 TAZs, high-income TAZs are a larger share of food-desert TAZs than low-income ones. This pattern is absent in cluster 1.
key_findings.numbers: Cluster 2: high-income share in food deserts 0.53 vs low-income 0.25 (p < 0.001). Cluster 1: 0.57 vs 0.47 (p = 0.76).

key_findings.finding: Flood extent does not differ significantly between the two recovery clusters. The authors argue that diminished access extends beyond flooding and is explained by sociodemographic and facility-distribution characteristics. This works against the abstract's claim that flooding disproportionally affects socially vulnerable populations.
key_findings.numbers: p = 0.33 for flooding extent, cluster 1 vs cluster 2; flood threshold 6.5% of TAZ area.

key_findings.finding: Discussion conclusion: during recovery, higher-income, lower-minority areas kept higher redundancy with smaller losses in proximity and rapidity. Lower-income, higher-minority areas had longer commutes and fewer store visits.
key_findings.numbers: None beyond the results above.

summary_md:
Esmalian et al. use StreetLight origin-destination trips and SafeGraph store locations to build bipartite networks linking traffic zones to grocery stores in Harris County during Hurricane Harvey (Aug-Sep 2017). The sample is 1,804 zones, 920 stores and 6,052 links. Each zone gets three access measures: redundancy (how many distinct stores its residents visit), rapidity (mean trip time) and proximity (mean trip distance). Each measure is expressed as percentage change from a weekday baseline and clustered with dynamic time warping (DTW).

In the preparation phase, high-income zones added more distinct stores than low-income zones. During recovery, the cluster that held up better had higher incomes and a lower minority share. The number of stores in a zone barely tracks the change in access: r = -0.06 for stores visited, -0.01 for trip time and -0.03 for trip distance. Food-desert status alone does not separate the groups. The paper's own test finds no flood-extent difference between the recovery clusters (p = 0.33), which undercuts the abstract's flooding claim.

The design is descriptive: one storm, one county, about six weeks. It reports no effect sizes. As extracted, Table 3 contradicts the text about which cluster is lower-income.

For Paul's systems this is an Adjacent paper with almost no transfer. It says nothing about lobbying, legislators, persuasion, turnout or influence networks. Its "network degree" counts distinct stores visited; it is not a centrality or influence measure. The only real point of contact: counting facilities on the supply side, or measuring plain distance, is a weak stand-in for the access people actually get. That bears weakly on Demographic Potential v3.0, which scores CU branch share and deposit share as "potential". It bears more weakly still on the Terrier turf planner, which ranks blocks by walking distance. Both transfers are by analogy across domains (grocery stores in a disaster vs CU branches and canvass walks in normal conditions). They are UNVERIFIED as evidence for either component.

bearings.paper_claim: How many facilities a zone has is a poor indicator of realized access. Correlation of stores per zone with the preparation-phase % change: stores visited r = -0.06 (p = 0.007), trip time r = -0.01 (p = 0.448), trip distance r = -0.03 (p = 0.100). Window: 24 Aug 2017. Denominator: Harris County zones in the analysis, N not reported. Food-desert status alone did not separate high- from low-income access.
bearings.paper_location: Results, Table 4, p.10; income x food desert, pp.9-10
bearings.system_side: The default Demographic Potential (footprint, ruling R7, D-035) scores a district on supply-side presence. Weights: CU employment LQ .30, establishment LQ .20, CU branch share .25, CU deposit share .25. It treats current footprint as the potential and makes no use-based or access-based measure.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak analogy only. The paper covers grocery trips in a disaster in one county, with access measured from mobility traces. Demographic Potential is a national, district-level market score under normal conditions. It is explicitly not a measure of support or access, and the footprint choice is an owner ruling. The paper's lesson (supply counts are not realized use) would matter only if footprint were read as members' or constituents' access to CUs. It does not challenge the owner's choice to treat footprint as potential. The same caution applies to the growth_room branch-whitespace term (demographic_potential.py:152).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-demographic-potential#Demographic Potential v3.0 (CU footprint, default)|Demographic Potential v3.0 (CU footprint, default)]]

bearings.paper_claim: "Approaches focused on physical distance ... is not a reliable measure of accessibility during disasters". Trip time and trip distance diverged by income group during preparation: lower-income zones with long baseline trips saw the largest increase in trip time, and high-income zones with short baseline trips saw the largest increase in distance.
bearings.paper_location: Introduction p.2 lines 70-72; Results, Preparation pp.8-9
bearings.system_side: The turf planner ranks blocks by preset value per 100 m of street length (length floored at 50 m). It grows a turf along connected streets with a 400 m jump allowance and routes on the TIGER street network, so cost is physical distance only.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over only if canvassing happens under disrupted conditions, such as flooding or road closures, when walk time stops tracking distance. For normal door-to-door canvassing on foot, distance is an adequate cost, and the paper offers no evidence against it. This is recorded as context, not a proposed change.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/terrier-canvass#Street-plan presets, turf planner and walk routing|Street-plan presets, turf planner and walk routing]]

gaps_exposed: Demographic Potential (footprint v3.0 and growth_room v2.1) uses only supply-side measures: branch and deposit share, LQ and whitespace. It has no measure of realized use, such as CU visits or membership per resident, to test whether presence equals access. The paper shows that facility counts track use changes only weakly (|r| <= 0.06). This matters only if footprint is ever read as access.

No component checks whether its scores differ across sociodemographic strata such as income or minority share. The paper's main finding is heterogeneity by income tertile. Any future use of a pooled district score over income strata should be quoted with those strata or labelled UNSTRATIFIED.
flags: The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). Its 'networks' are bipartite zone-to-store trip graphs, and 'degree' means distinct stores visited, not influence, closeness or access probability. Do not port its 'weighted degree' language into Melange SNA wording (D-025).

The causal language in the paper ('disproportionately exacerbated', 'flooding disproportionally affects') is not supported by its descriptive design, and its own test finds no flood-extent difference between clusters (p = 0.33). Do not cite it for causal claims.
As extracted, Table 3 contradicts the text: the highest-redundancy cluster shows a higher per-capita income ($36,008, starred) and fewer stores (0.67). Check against the PDF before quoting.
The normal-period window is inconsistent: 5-16 Aug in the text vs 7-16 Aug in the Fig. 3 caption. Any figure quoted from it must name which window it uses.
Both bearings are this agent's analogy across domains. They stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062).
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper, and no component lists it among his citations. Nothing in his positions to agree or disagree with, and no stale note to update. His one related idea is the state or industry-presence targeting layer, which became Demographic Potential (Huneeus & Kim). The paper gently cautions that presence differs from realized access. It does not touch the owner ruling that footprint is the potential.

related.why: Hargittai documents sampling biases in big data drawn from digital traces. Esmalian rests on StreetLight cell/GPS traces with an undescribed penetration rate and black-box home-zone inference, which is exactly that kind of bias. Read together, this limits how far its findings by income can be trusted.

Both papers infer movement cost or access from observed movement rather than straight-line distance: Zeller estimates resistance to movement with step and path selection functions, and Esmalian uses trip time vs trip distance. Both are relevant to any travel-cost weighting in the Terrier turf planner.

meta.title: Heuristic centrality methods challenge greedy optimization in influence maximization

extraction.title: Heuristic centrality methods challenge greedy optimization in influence maximization
extraction.document_type: Journal article: empirical comparative study of eight influence maximization algorithms on simulated Independent Cascade diffusion over Facebook subgraphs (open access, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)
extraction.coverage: Read the full text file (1352 lines, about 91k characters, pages 1-18 including references and declarations) in four 250-line chunks plus a final chunk; no section skipped. Metadata hint checked against the text: title, authors, venue, DOI and year all match, so no correction was needed. paul_markup is empty because the task listed no markup files; no sidecar or annotation files were searched for or read. The text is a PDF extraction, so page numbers are inferred from running footers (page 1 = lines 1-46; page 8 = lines 455-551; page 15 = lines 1081-1148).
extraction.research_question: Do the theoretical guarantees of influence maximization algorithms (greedy CELF++, sampling-based RIS and IMM) hold in practice, and how do they compare with simple centrality heuristics (Degree, PageRank, Betweenness, Dangling, GCCDC) on spread quality, runtime and scaling under the Independent Cascade model on real social network subgraphs?
extraction.theory: Influence maximization is NP-hard under IC and LT (Kempe et al. 2003, ref 12). The influence function is submodular, so greedy selection gives a (1-1/e) approximation (Nemhauser et al. 1978, ref 15). CELF and CELF++ use lazy evaluation to speed up greedy without changing that guarantee. RIS and IMM recast the problem as coverage of reverse-reachable sets with sampling bounds. Centrality heuristics carry no guarantee and are justified as cheap structural proxies. The paper's framing: asymptotic guarantees can diverge from practice because hidden constants, network structure and implementation matter (p.4, lines 260-269; p.13, lines 948-961).
extraction.data: Source: Facebook ego network from the SNAP collection, 4,039 nodes and 88,234 undirected edges (p.6, lines 402-404). Sampled subgraphs: 200, 500, 800 and 1000 nodes per Methods and Table 2 (p.6, p.8); the abstract instead says 200, 400, 600, 800 and 1,000 nodes (p.1). Unit: one seed set per algorithm, size and run. Count: 8 algorithms x 4 sizes x 10 independent runs (seeds 42-51) = 320 seed sets, each scored by 50 Monte Carlo IC simulations (p.6, lines 411-434). No time period; a static snapshot of the 2014 SNAP dataset.
extraction.method: Eight algorithms, implemented in Python 3.8 with NumPy 1.21 and NetworkX 2.6 (p.8): CELF++ (50 MC per marginal-gain estimate); RIS with theta = min(10000, 50n); IMM with epsilon = 0.2; Degree; PageRank (damping 0.85, power iteration, tolerance 1e-6, max 100 iterations); Betweenness (Brandes); Dangling centrality; GCCDC (p.4-6). Diffusion: IC with uniform p = 0.1 on all edges; seed budget k = 10. Subgraphs drawn by importance sampling: node importance is the average of normalised degree centrality and normalised PageRank; top-ranked nodes plus their highest-importance neighbours are kept to keep the subgraph connected (p.6, lines 402-410). Evaluation: mean spread over 50 MC simulations per seed set; 10 runs per configuration; mean, SD, min, max and CV reported; wall-clock seconds; spread per second as efficiency (p.7-8). Significance: paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction (alpha 0.05), with Mann-Whitney U said to give the same results (p.7-8, p.8).
extraction.identification: None in a causal sense. This is a controlled simulation benchmark: algorithms are compared on identical subgraphs under the same IC settings, and seeds are paired across runs for the t-tests. No natural experiment or instrument is used.
extraction.scope: One real-world network (Facebook ego network subgraphs) at 200-1000 nodes; one diffusion model (IC, uniform p = 0.1); one seed budget (k = 10); undirected graphs only. Not tested: directed, weighted or temporal networks; other diffusion models; large-scale graphs; deep RL or GNN methods. The paper says the sampled subgraphs have degree exponent above 3 (p.6, lines 408-409).

key_findings.finding: CELF++ performs far below the other algorithms at 1000 nodes (about 12.9% of IMM), despite its (1-1/e) guarantee. The authors attribute this mainly to only 50 MC simulations per estimate and Python implementation, not to an algorithmic flaw.
key_findings.location: Results p.8 (lines 473-486); Discussion p.13 (lines 948-955); Conclusion p.15-16
key_findings.numbers: CELF++ 122.95 +/- 24.37 vs IMM 954.90 +/- 1.27; ratio 12.9%; Delta 831.95, t = -107.78, p < 0.001. Abstract (p.1) says 11.2%, which conflicts.

key_findings.finding: IMM is best at 1000 nodes and RIS is close behind. The IMM-RIS gap is small but significant.
PageRank and Betweenness are statistically indistinguishable and reach about 96.5% of IMM spread at 1000 nodes, at 0.4 s and 8.8 s respectively.
key_findings.location: Results p.8-9 (lines 474-476, 495-499); Table 3 p.11; efficiency p.10 (lines 658-666); Discussion p.13 and p.15
key_findings.numbers: PageRank 921.78 +/- 3.28; Betweenness 921.80 +/- 3.34; Delta -0.02, t = -0.01, p = 0.99; PageRank vs IMM Delta 33.12, t = 26.97, p < 0.001. The paper states 96.3% in the abstract, Discussion and Conclusion, but 921.78/954.90 = 96.5%. Stated 794x runtime speed-up: 323.5/0.4 = 809x from the paper's own times.

key_findings.finding: Degree, GCCDC and Dangling form a lower cluster around 80-85% of IMM spread. Dangling is lowest. GCCDC does not improve on Degree at 1000 nodes.
key_findings.location: Results p.8 (lines 475-477); Algorithm-specific observations p.12 (lines 893-908); Broader Discussion p.15 (lines 1123-1129)
key_findings.numbers: Degree 810.87 +/- 6.77; GCCDC 811.59 +/- 5.00; Dangling 797.44 +/- 12.05 (CV up to 6.24%). Degree vs Dangling t = 2.67, p < 0.05; GCCDC vs Dangling t = 2.90, p < 0.05.

key_findings.finding: Sampling methods (IMM, RIS) have very low variance and scale near-linearly. Heuristics have moderate CVs. CELF++ is unstable, with a non-monotone trajectory.
key_findings.location: Scalability p.9 (lines 558-576); Algorithm-specific observations p.11-12 (lines 868-875); Fig. 4 p.10
key_findings.numbers: IMM CV 0.07-0.17%; RIS CV 0.13-0.23%; Betweenness CV 0.16-0.36%; PageRank 0.14-0.25%; Degree 0.66-2.59%; CELF++ CV rose to 71.5% at 500 nodes (p.10, line 646).

key_findings.finding: Growth from 200 to 1000 nodes is close to proportional for most methods. The text and Table 4 disagree for some entries.
key_findings.numbers: Text: IMM +402%, RIS +399%, PageRank +403%, Degree +411%, CELF++ +633%. Table 4: IMM +402%, RIS +400%, PageRank +404%, Degree +410%, CELF++ +740%. CELF++ at 500 nodes is 4.56 in the text and 4.91 in Table 2.

key_findings.finding: Efficiency ranking: PageRank 2,304 spread/s; Degree 2,027; Dangling 1,994; GCCDC 279.86; Betweenness 104.75; RIS 14.68; IMM 2.95; CELF++ 0.18 (all at 1000 nodes).
key_findings.location: Computational efficiency p.10 (lines 658-664); Fig. 3 caption p.9
key_findings.numbers: PageRank 921.78 spread / 0.4 s; IMM 954.90 / 323.5 s; CELF++ 122.95 / 688.4 s max runtime. RIS vs PageRank: 3.3% lower spread for 162x runtime (p.10-11).

key_findings.finding: Extrapolated runtimes to 10,000 nodes are reported but were not measured.
key_findings.numbers: RIS about 795 s; IMM about 3970 s; CELF++ about 840 s at 1000 nodes and over 8,400 s at 10,000 nodes (linear extrapolation). The limitations section also quotes PageRank at about 5 s at 10,000 nodes, a figure not given in the Discussion. Linear scaling from RIS's 64.9 s would give about 649 s, not 795 s.

Across 10 runs: mean, SD, min, max, coefficient of variation

summary_md:
Almazaydeh et al. compare eight influence-maximization methods under the Independent Cascade (IC) model. The graphs are Facebook ego-network subgraphs of 200 to 1,000 nodes, with uniform p = 0.1, k = 10 seeds, 10 runs and 50 Monte Carlo (MC) simulations per seed set. At 1,000 nodes, IMM is best (954.90) and RIS is close behind (952.53, five times faster). PageRank and Betweenness cannot be told apart (about 921.8, or 96.5% of IMM; the paper itself says 96.3%), and PageRank runs in 0.4 s. Degree, GCCDC and Dangling reach about 80-85% of IMM. CELF++ collapses to 12.9% of IMM (the abstract says 11.2%), with a CV of up to 71.5%. The authors blame only 50 MC simulations per marginal estimate plus a Python implementation, but they never test that explanation. The study has several internal inconsistencies: subgraph sizes, percentages, the 794x speed-up and the extrapolated runtimes do not match the paper's own tables.

This paper is already wired into Melange. `fec/engine/mc_stability_check.py` names it as its motivation. The skill library cites it to argue that the frontier's MC=20 greedy is safe because common random numbers (CRN) mean every candidate is compared under the same draws. That reasoning is sound for comparing marginals. The problem is that the recorded pass is older than a 2026-10-01 fix. The pass (MEA-7, holistic graph: 100% at MC=100, 98% across RNG seeds) was measured before QME fix 3. Before that fix, the splitmix keys did not depend on SEED, so the 'different RNG seed' runs reused the same edge and seed-activation draws. The MC=100 leg still holds, though it shares its first 20 iterations with production. The cross-seed leg did not test independent draws.

The paper's other point, that cheap centrality gets within a few percent of IMM, suggests a cheap ablation the system lacks: run a PageRank, degree or Katz-Bonacich seed baseline through the same CRN cascade. It would be an ablation only, because stance gating and seed activation are things centrality cannot see. The joint optimizer is untouched by this paper. It is deterministic (no MC), so the CELF++ failure mode cannot occur there.

extraction.research_question: Does learning separate neural architectures per user profile (gender, or age split at 30) improve automatic self-reported Big Five personality recognition over one generic model, using multimodal behavioural features from dyadic interactions?
extraction.theory: Personality computing built on the Big Five (OCEAN) model. Premise: self-reported traits and the way traits are expressed in nonverbal behaviour differ by gender, age and culture, so one-fits-all models may be suboptimal. No formal theory is tested.
extraction.data: UDIVA dataset: 188 dyadic face-to-face interactions, 147 participants, 90.5 hours of recordings, 55.1 percent male, ages 4 to 84, 22 nationalities (68 percent Spain), five interaction contexts (talk, animals game, Lego building, ghost blitz card game, gaze events). Unit of analysis: one-minute per-participant segments (25 fps, 1,500 frames). Outcome: self-reported Big Five scores. Model trained on challenge train and validation partitions; evaluated on the unseen challenge test partition. Test-set N and profile subgroup sizes are not reported.
extraction.method: Per-modality features: FaceBody landmark mean and SD (552 dims); talk-turn duration (5), content (5), sentiment (10, Spanish-only library), speech rate (5); SBERT sentence embeddings; MFCC-20 band-energy statistics. For each profile (female, male; age 30 or under, over 30) and each modality, Auto-Keras neural architecture search (network morphism with Bayesian optimisation), 100 trials, up to 1,000 epochs, Adam optimiser, MSE loss, early stopping patience 30, 85/15 train/validation split, default start of two 32-unit dense layers. Decision fusion: per-minute scores averaged over sessions, then modality predictions averaged, using the best two modalities or all modalities. Comparison against generic models and challenge-team results.
extraction.scope: Population: adult and minor participants in dyadic video interactions, mostly Spanish-speaking (dominant language Spanish, then Catalan and English). Institution: ChaLearn LAP DYAD challenge at ICCV 2021, automatic self-reported personality track. Era: 2021-2022 challenge; collection date of UDIVA not stated in text.
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. Profile-specific models are compared with a generic model and challenge entries on one fixed test split. No significance tests, intervals, or repeated-seed variance are reported in the text.

summary_md: Salam, Manoranjan, Jiang and Celiktutan (PMLR 173, 2022) ask whether one Big Five recognizer for everyone is worse than separate models for each user profile. They test this on UDIVA dyadic video (188 interactions, 147 participants, 90.5 hours, mostly Spanish speakers). For each profile (female/male; age 30 or under/over 30) and each modality, they run an Auto-Keras architecture search. Modalities are face/body landmarks, talk-turn duration, content, sentiment and speech rate, SBERT text and MFCC audio. Predictions are then fused at the decision level. The outcome is self-reported OCEAN, scored by mean squared error. Fusing the two best modalities within each gender gives an average MSE of 0.690. Age-wise fusion gives 0.796 and generic fusion 0.818. Dyadformer scores 0.722 and the authors' earlier challenge ensemble 0.769. Almost all of the gain comes from the gender split. Age adds little, and in the generic setting fusion barely beats the best single modality (0.818 vs 0.820). Turn-taking features beat face/body features (0.874 vs 1.325). The evidence is thin. There is one challenge test split, with no test N, subgroup sizes, intervals or seed variance. Gender is binary, the fairness claim is untested, and the text and Table 1 disagree on the headline number. For Paul's systems, the transferable lesson is narrow. Acoustic features whose signal partly is speaker sex need sex-conditioned comparison. The Melange audio lane already ran a Salam-style check: pace and volume are sex-clean, while pitch variability and jitter are not. But the semitone-SD fix sits on an unmerged branch. The paper gives no basis for building per-sex trait models for legislators, whose criteria are expert ratings, not self-reports. All transfer here is UNVERIFIED.

extraction.document_type: Journal article (simulation-based algorithm analysis, multi-agent path finding / robotics)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in three chunks (extraction lines 0-616, covering all 43371 chars): front matter, abstract, introduction, related work, methodology, environments and metrics, results (Tables 1-2, Figures 2-6), conclusion, and the complete reference list. Paul's markup: all 4 annotations in the _annots JSON read (all on PDF page 1, journal p.20; none has a note). Metadata hint was correct on title, DOI, year, venue and author surnames; full author names and dates were added from the paper. Checked for networks, lobbying, allocation, elections, persuasion/turnout, legislators and text measurement: none appear in the paper (path-finding here is robot routing only). The paper has no limitations section. It does not describe hardware, software, code availability, number of simulation runs, or numeric environment parameters. Quotes limited to one per the copyright rule, which overrides the 3-quote request; Paul's highlighted text is paraphrased, not reproduced.
extraction.research_question: Does replacing A* with D* Lite as the low-level single-agent planner inside Conflict-Based Search (CBS) reduce computation time and nodes explored, while keeping path length, for multi-agent path finding in dynamic environments (moving or appearing obstacles, moving agents)?
extraction.theory: No formal theory is developed. The paper rests on the two-level CBS framework (high-level conflict tree plus low-level single-agent planner; Sharon et al. 2012) and on D* Lite's incremental replanning, which reuses earlier search results when costs change (Koenig and Likhachev 2002). The D* Lite priority key is written out in Eq. (1) and the one-step lookahead rhs(s) in Eq. (2); Eq. (3) gives each agent's path as a D* Lite call on graph G=(V,E) under CBS constraints. No hypotheses are stated.
extraction.data: Simulated 3D voxel-grid multi-agent path-planning scenarios with random start and goal positions and randomized obstacle positions and movement, regenerated for each iteration (Sec. 4, p.24-25). Three environment types are described: Static Maze, Dynamic Open Field (sparse moving obstacles), and Crowded Warehouse (dense, randomly appearing and disappearing obstacles). Unit of analysis: a multi-agent instance (per-scenario run). Number of runs or instances (N) is not reported. The only instance with reported detail is 15 agents (Figs. 3-6, Table 1). The conclusion also cites a 3-agent case and a 6-agent case with no table or figure. No real-world data, no human sample, no time period beyond simulation.
extraction.method: Simulation comparison of two low-level planners inside CBS: A* (baseline CBS-A*) versus D* Lite (CBS-D*Lite), each with 4-point (4 directions in 3D) and 8-point (4 plus diagonals) neighbour search. Pseudocode is in Fig. 1 (p.23). Metrics: execution time (s) to compute paths for all agents, nodes explored (expansions by the low-level planner), and average path length per agent (units). Results are reported as means across test scenarios (Table 2) with per-case values for 15 agents (Table 1). Qualitative claims on adaptability, conflict-resolution responsiveness and scalability are drawn from the same runs (p.28). No replication count, variance, confidence intervals or significance tests are reported. Implementation language, hardware and random seeds are not stated.
extraction.identification: None in the causal or statistical sense. The design is an algorithm-versus-algorithm benchmark on simulated instances. The two planners are compared on the same scenario type, but the paper does not state that instances were paired across planners, nor how many instances went into the Table 2 averages.
extraction.scope: Population: simulated 3D multi-agent path-planning instances (warehouse, swarm, search-and-rescue and autonomous-vehicle settings motivate the work). Institutions: Electrical Engineering and Mechatronics departments at Suez Canal University and German University in Cairo. Era: received April 2025, published October 2025. Not tested on physical robots or real facilities.

summary_md:
Abdel-Rahman et al. (2025) swap A* for D* Lite as the low-level single-agent planner inside Conflict-Based Search (CBS), a two-level multi-agent path-finding method. They test it on simulated 3D voxel grids with moving or appearing obstacles. In the paper's Table 2 averages, execution time falls from 5.575 s to 0.04 s and nodes explored fall from 2142 to 250.5, while D* Lite paths come out about 0.8% longer (15.73 vs 15.6). The paper labels that change -0.8% and says optimality is kept. The evidence is thin:
- The number of runs is not reported, and there is no variance or significance test.
- The 5.575 s average does not match its own Table 1, whose values average to 4.575 s.
- The node reduction comes entirely from the 4-neighbour case. With 8 neighbours, D* Lite explores more nodes than A* (198 vs 178).
- The scalability claim rests on one 15-agent case.
- Nothing in the paper concerns legislators, lobbying or social networks.

For Paul's systems, the paper is relevant only to path-finding, as a possible design pattern rather than as evidence. D* Lite earns its speed by reusing earlier search work when edge costs change. None of the built routers do that: the cosponsor route finder, the dashboard recruitment chain and the staffer route search each rebuild every search from scratch on a fixed graph. On a 533-member graph a full recompute is already cheap, so the paper's compute savings do not transfer. Its useful idea is conceptual. When a planned recruitment ask fails or a member's stance changes, the route should be repaired, not abandoned. The dashboard's chain-hold figure currently assumes no rerouting at all. Paul's addendum makes D* Lite and LPA* the operational layer, and this paper is too weak to support that choice on its own.

bearings.paper_claim: Replacing A* with incremental D* Lite inside CBS cuts mean execution time from 5.575 s to 0.04 s (99.2%) and nodes explored from 2142 to 250.5 (88.3%), at about 0.8% longer paths (15.73 vs 15.6). However, the 8-point case explores more nodes with D* Lite (198 vs 178). The number of runs is not reported.
bearings.system_side: The route finder is a static greedy builder on the shared build_P kernel. It reruns build_route from scratch for each of the five lambda values and keeps a Pareto front over cost, expected cosponsors and risk. A per-recruiter whip cap of K=5 is the only shared-resource constraint. MOPBD* is named in the docstring as a concept only. The code does no incremental replanning and no repair when an edge or stance changes.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The speedup does not transfer. It was measured on 3D voxel grids with moving obstacles, while this graph has 533 nodes and recomputing it costs very little. What carries over is the idea of repairing a route when a member joins, declines or changes stance, rather than rebuilding it. The K=5 whip cap loosely resembles a CBS conflict over a shared resource, but CBS resolves conflicts between agents competing for space and time, not recruiter bandwidth. Treat the paper as a design pointer only (weak, single-source, unreplicated, UNVERIFIED).

bearings.transfer_conditions: The extension would need an observed event: a failed ask or a stance move that changes edge probabilities while a campaign is under way. Only then would incremental repair, or simply recomputing the route, give a reroute-aware chain hold. The paper gives no evidence about recruitment success. Edge p values are heuristic kernel outputs, not ask-success probabilities (D-025 wording applies).

bearings.system_side: The router runs bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0 to a virtual sink, plus Yen loopless alternatives. It runs one search per request on a fixed evidence snapshot, with no work caps (exact proof of the optimal route). The latency lane kept one-way Dijkstra without a heuristic and deferred ALT.
bearings.transfer_conditions: D* Lite pays off only when costs change between successive queries on the same graph. Each staffer request starts on a fixed snapshot, so incremental search buys little unless the sidecar starts updating evidence in place between queries. The current design, exact and stateless, has no gap that this paper fills.

gaps_exposed: No incremental or repair-based replanning in any built router: cosponsor_route.py, the dashboard buildPath/chainHold, and the staffer routes all recompute from scratch. A route is never updated when a planned ask fails or a stance changes during a campaign.
chainHold explicitly assumes no rerouting, so it understates chain success in any setting where failed hops are re-planned. Nothing models a reroute-aware chain probability.

There is no multi-agent conflict layer. Several recruiters or lobbyists working the same targets at once (overlapping asks, the same member asked by two chains) are handled only by the per-recruiter K cap, not by a CBS-style search over conflicts.
flags: Internal numeric inconsistency: Table 2 reports a CBS-A* mean of 5.575 s, but Table 1's values (8.64 and 0.51) average to 4.575 s. The path-length change is labelled -0.8%, yet D* Lite paths are about 0.8% longer.

The paper is weak as evidence: N is not reported, there is no variance or significance testing, the hardware and seeds are not stated, and scalability rests on a single 15-agent case. The 3-agent and 6-agent figures appear only in the conclusion. Do not quote the 99.2% figure as a general D* Lite speedup.
The node-reduction result reverses in the 8-point neighbour case (198 vs 178), so the claim that D* Lite uniformly reduces nodes explored is false within the paper's own data.

extraction.research_question: Three questions stated on p.5 (Introduction, lines 266-286): (1) Are there voice features related to self-reported Big Five scores (externalization)? (2) Are the voice features related to externalization the same as those related to the accuracy of close-other and expert judgments? (3) Can personality dimensions be predicted from voice recorded with ordinary devices in controlled but not restricted speech, so the approach could fit Asynchronous Video Interviews and personnel selection?
extraction.theory: Brunswick lens model as adapted by Scherer (1978): traits are externalized through objectively measurable speech variables (distal cues), perceived by listeners as proximal cues that ground attributions (p.2, lines 80-86). Brown and Bradshaw (1985) three facets: accuracy, externalization, attribution; this study tests externalization and accuracy (p.5, lines 258-265). Big Five framework; the authors also draw on the Cannata et al. (2022) call to join psychological personality-judgment research and personality computing (p.3, lines 156-163). Authors argue speech reveals the self (Allport and Cantril 1934; Allport 1937) (p.5, lines 238-239). No formal hypothesis is stated; the authors describe the study as exploratory.
extraction.data: Unit: individual participant (interview recording). N = 100 female participants, split into Sample 1 (n = 78 female psychology students, aged 18-27, M = 20.18) and Sample 2 (n = 44 female participants, aged 18-54, M = 29.42) (p.5, lines 289-292). NOTE: the two sample sizes sum to 122, not 100; the text does not reconcile this. Recruitment: the first author's School of Psychology participant pool at Universidad Autonoma de Madrid, students paid in extra credit (p.5, lines 296-299). Recording period: not stated; the only date is the IRB approval of June 2016 (p.17, lines 1311-1313). Procedure: group session (60-item NEO-FFI, Spanish adaptation), individual interview in the following two weeks, about 7 min per session (p.7, lines 402-410). Audio: WAV, 16 kHz, mono, 16-bit; manually selected open-answer segments, mean 172.8 s (SD 102 s), range 49 s to 15 min; total 4 h 48 min (p.7, lines 414-430). Two different microphones were used for Sample 1 and Sample 2 (p.16). Data available only on request, for privacy reasons (p.17, line 1315). Expert rating subset: N = 20 videos for inter-rater ICC (p.7).
extraction.method: Voice features: the AVEC 2011 emotion feature set extracted with OpenSMILE 2.3, 1941 features (25 energy/spectral LLDs x 42 functionals, 6 voicing LLDs x 32, 25 delta energy/spectral x 23, 6 delta voicing x 19, 10 voiced/unvoiced durations) (p.6, lines 311-323). Analysis 1 (externalization and accuracy): Pearson-type correlation of all 1941 features with each Big Five score from three criteria (self-report, close-other rubric, expert VAS), then reporting the top features per trait in Sample 1 (Table 4). Replication: the top-correlated self-report feature per trait was re-examined in Sample 2 (Section 3.1.6). Analysis 2 (prediction): for each of five traits, the five highest-correlated features were used; scores were binned into low/medium/high at the 25th and 75th percentiles of training data; random forest classifier (scikit-learn, n_estimators = 20, other defaults); leave-one-out with 100 folds (99 train / 1 test). SVM and multiple linear regression were tried but not reported because random forests did better (p.13, lines 1005-1010). Software: Python with Pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn (p.8). The text does not say whether the five features were selected inside each LOO fold or on the full sample; this is a reviewer note, not a stated fact, and it bears on whether the reported accuracies are out-of-sample. The text also does not name the correlation type or any multiple-comparison correction across 1941 features.
extraction.scope: Population: adult female Spanish participants recruited at one Madrid university; Sample 1 is mostly students aged 18-27. Institution: Universidad Autonoma de Madrid (School of Psychology and Polytechnic School of Engineering). Era: collection date not stated; published 2024. Setting: semi-structured interview simulating a job interview (warm-up questions, then self-description, career, and a 15-year future question; p.7 lines 418-424). Sex: all participants are female, which the authors treat as a sample restriction (p.16). Constructs: Big Five self-report, close-other judgments, and zero-acquaintance expert ratings from video plus audio.

key_findings.finding: Close-other ratings correlate with self-report on all Big Five dimensions except Openness. Expert ratings match self-report only for Conscientiousness and Extraversion.
key_findings.numbers: Close-other vs self, significant range 0.32 (Neuroticism) to 0.51 (Extraversion). Expert vs self: 'Responsibility' 0.34 and Extraversion 0.31; both significant, the rest not.

key_findings.finding: Single voice features correlate moderately with personality ratings in Sample 1. The top correlation per trait and criterion is given in Table 4.
key_findings.numbers: Self: Extraversion 0.47 (mfcc_sma[3]_lpgain), Neuroticism 0.37, Openness 0.36, Agreeableness -0.33, Conscientiousness 0.30. Experts: Extraversion 0.48, Neuroticism -0.47, Conscientiousness 0.44, Openness -0.36, Agreeableness 0.35. Close others: Openness -0.41, Agreeableness -0.41, Neuroticism 0.32, Extraversion 0.40 (text says 0.40 in one sentence and 0.41 in the next), Conscientiousness -0.30.

key_findings.finding: Expert ratings showed the strongest voice correlates; the authors read this as expert judgments tracking voice cues more than close-other judgments do.
key_findings.numbers: Largest correlations with acoustic features came from the non-acquainted expert. Expert Extraversion accuracy 60% was the best prediction cell (Table 6).

key_findings.finding: The feature-level correlations did not replicate across samples. Sample 2 (self-report only) gave different features, although of similar magnitude.
key_findings.numbers: Sample 2 top features: Neuroticism mfcc_sma[1]_percentile99.0 r=0.52; Extraversion F0final_sma_quartile3 r=0.46 (p=0.002); Openness mfcc_sma[3]_kurtosis r=0.52; Agreeableness mfcc_sma[2]_skewness r=-0.46 (p=0.002); Conscientiousness mfcc_sma_de[7]_kurtosis r=-0.53. Authors say the results 'did not coincide'.

key_findings.finding: Three-class (low/medium/high) classification from the top-5 voice features gives overall accuracy above the 33% chance rate for most criteria, but not above the 50% majority-class baseline for self-report.
key_findings.numbers: All-cases accuracy (%): Self N 50, E 46, O 46, A 53, C 43. Expert N 57, E 60, O 57, A 56, C 53. Close others N 54, E 57, O 45, A 52, C 54. Chance 33%; a constant central-class prediction gives 50% because the central band holds 50% of cases (p.14).

key_findings.finding: Within-class accuracy is highest for medium-trait cases and lower for low and high cases. Some cells are extreme: the Conscientiousness high-trait cell for self-report is 4.1%.
key_findings.numbers: Medium-trait accuracy ranges 47.4% to 81.1%; examples: close-other Neuroticism medium 76.4%, expert Neuroticism medium 81.1%. Self-report Conscientiousness high 4.1%, Extraversion high 18.2%. Close-other Conscientiousness low 0%, high 64.3%.

key_findings.finding: Expert zero-acquaintance rating reliability was moderate to strong on four dimensions and low on Openness. This rating is the criterion that the authors say voice predicts best.
key_findings.numbers: ICC on N=20 videos: Emotional Adjustment 0.70, Extraversion 0.73, Agreeableness 0.74, Conscientiousness 0.82, Openness 0.23. Experts discussed disagreements and re-rated Openness.

key_findings.finding: The Discussion's numbers do not match the Results. It says the highest trait correlations were Neuroticism 0.38 and Extraversion 0.40, and that the predictions range 0.3 to 0.4. Results and Table 4 report 0.47 to 0.48 for Extraversion.
key_findings.location: Abstract p.1 (lines 45-47); Discussion p.14 (lines 1129-1132); Results p.8-10 (lines 459-460, 466, 475)
key_findings.numbers: Discussion: N 0.38, E 0.40. Results: E 0.47 (self), 0.48 (expert). Text claims all correlations p<0.001 with a maximum of 0.50, but Table 4 shows p = 0.0013, 0.002, 0.004 and 0.01 for some cells and a maximum of 0.48.

key_findings.finding: The authors compare the voice results with facial-expression work and conclude voice alone is more limited; they call personality prediction a multimodal task.
key_findings.numbers: Voice best case about 60% accuracy vs over 75% for facial-expression work by Gavrilescu (ref 56, cited as [56]).

limitations: Sample: 100 participants, all female, mostly psychology students (age 18-27 in Sample 1). Authors say the group is homogeneous in age and personality, so extreme trait values are unlikely, limiting external validity (p.16).
Effect sizes are moderate and may not hold in larger or more varied samples; the authors say they should be read cautiously (p.16).
No cross-cultural sampling; the authors say cultural norms may change how traits are externalized through voice (p.16).

Confounders: noise in some recordings; two different microphones for Sample 1 and Sample 2, which the authors say may explain the lack of replication; colds, fatigue and emotional state could act as latent variables (p.16).
Only vocal aspects were analyzed. Fluency (pauses, discontinuities), morphology/syntax, conversational behavior, facial expression, body language and movement were not (p.17).
Feature interpretability is weak: most top features are MFCC or LPC coefficients whose meaning is unclear, and the top features did not replicate across samples (pp.12-15).

No explicit power analysis. The authors say N = 100 gives 80% power for correlations near 0.2 (p.5, lines 300-304). Many features (1941) raise the risk of spurious correlation; the authors used two samples to check consistency (p.5).
Expert Openness reliability was low (ICC 0.23 on 20 videos) (p.7).

Internal inconsistencies found in the text, not reconciled by the authors: Sample sizes 78 + 44 = 122 vs N = 100; Discussion correlation values (0.38/0.40) vs Results (0.47/0.48); Extraversion close-other r given as both 0.40 and 0.41; 'all p < 0.001' vs Table 4 p-values up to 0.01; 'one of two experts' vs both experts rating videos (p.7).
Data are available only on request for privacy reasons, so the results cannot be reproduced from the paper alone (p.17).

Prediction set-up: the text does not say whether feature selection (top-5 by correlation) was done inside each leave-one-out fold; this must be checked before accepting the 43-60% accuracies as out-of-sample.
measures: Big Five self-report: NEO-FFI, 60-item Spanish adaptation (Cordero et al. 2008), completed in a group session (p.7).

Close-other judgments: 3-point (low/medium/high) rubric for 5 dimensions, completed by a relative or close friend; adapted from the NEO-FFI manual summary sheet (p.7; rubric in Supplementary Materials).

Expert zero-acquaintance ratings: 15 cm visual analog scale per Big Five dimension, scored as cm from the 0 mark, based on watching the full video (p.7). Two experienced PhD assessors (one female, one male; over 25 years of experience); calibrated to 100% agreement on cues before rating.
Inter-rater ICC on 20 videos: Emotional Adjustment 0.70, Extraversion 0.73, Agreeableness 0.74, Conscientiousness 0.82, Openness 0.23 (p.7).
Voice features: OpenSMILE AVEC 2011 emotion set, 1941 functionals (LLDs, deltas, voicing, durations) (p.6, Tables 1-2).
Dependent variable for prediction: low/medium/high classes at training-set 25th and 75th percentiles (p.13).
references_of_note: Ambady and Rosenthal 1992, Psychol. Bull. 111:256 (ref 3): thin-slice meta-analysis, overall accuracy 0.39 in zero-acquaintance predictions of outcomes. Relevant to the persuasion/accuracy theme.

Mairesse, Walker, Mehl and Moore 2007, J. Artif. Intell. Res. 30:457 (ref 14): automatic recognition of personality from linguistic cues in conversation and text. Closest text-measurement precedent in the reference list.
Van Zant and Berger 2020, J. Pers. Soc. Psychol. 118:661 (ref 23): 'How the voice persuades'; paralinguistic cues (pitch, volume) enhance persuasion. Only persuasion-related work the paper cites.
Breil, Osterholz, Nestler and Back 2021 (ref 24): review of 32 studies, up to 39 non-verbal cues, correlations with Big Five traits.
Cannata et al. 2022, Technol. Mind Behav. 3:1 (ref 27): framework linking psychological and AI personality research; the paper's stated bridge.
Hickman et al. 2022, J. Appl. Psychol. 107:1323 (ref 50): reliability, validity and generalizability of automated video-interview personality assessments.
Koutsoumpis et al. 2024, Comput. Hum. Behav. 154:108128 (ref 49): audio signals predict self-report and expert-rated traits in asynchronous video interviews.
Hosoda, Stone-Romero and Coats 2003 (ref 60): meta-analysis of physical attractiveness effects on job outcomes; cited for recruiter attribution bias.
Youyou, Kosinski and Stillwell 2015, PNAS 112:1036 (ref 57): computer-based personality judgments more accurate than human judgments.
Eyben et al. 2010 (ref 39, OpenSMILE) and Schuller et al. 2011 (ref 38, AVEC 2011 feature set): the feature pipeline used.
Mohammadi and Vinciarelli 2012, IEEE Trans. Affect. Comput. 3:273 (ref 41): automatic personality perception from prosodic features; Speaker Personality Corpus source.
Pennebaker and King 1999 (ref 59) and Argamon et al. 2005 (ref 58): lexical and linguistic-style predictors of personality; the text-based tradition the authors contrast with voice.
Marrero et al. 2022, Acta Psychol. 230:103740 (ref 21): voice samples predict self-reported traits (about 10% of variance).

short_quotes.quote: Voice features are related to the externalization of individuals' personality characteristics.

extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The design is cross-sectional: correlations between acoustic features and three personality criteria (Sample 1, with Sample 2 as a replication for self-report), then leave-one-out random-forest classification on N = 100. No instrument, quasi-experiment or manipulation. Out-of-sample validity depends on whether feature selection was inside each fold, which the text does not state.
extraction.theory_note: The paper treats personality as externalized through vocal cues and perceived by judges. Accuracy and externalization are kept separate (Brown and Bradshaw 1985).

summary_md:
Rubio, Aguado, Toledano and Fernandez-Gallego (Sensors 2024) recorded about 7-minute mock job interviews with Spanish women, nearly all students. They extracted 1,941 OpenSMILE AVEC-2011 acoustic functionals and correlated them with Big Five scores from three sources: NEO-FFI self-report, close-other ratings and zero-acquaintance expert ratings. In Sample 1 (n=78), the best single feature reached r of about 0.30-0.48 per trait. Expert ratings tracked voice most closely (E 0.48, N -0.47). The paper also says N=100, but its two samples add to 122.

The key result is negative: the top features did not replicate in Sample 2 (n=44). The authors suggest a microphone change may explain this. For prediction, the top five features fed a random forest that sorted people into low, medium or high on each trait, scored by leave-one-out. Self-report accuracy was 43-53%, no better than the 50% you get by always guessing "medium". Expert ratings did best, at 53-60%. The paper never says whether the top five features were chosen inside each fold, so even those figures may be optimistic. The Discussion's numbers also contradict the Results (0.38/0.40 vs 0.47/0.48).

For Melange, the paper backs the audio lane's existing verdict rather than reopening it. The lane uses a related toolkit (eGeMAPS v02 from openSMILE), and its audio Neuroticism (N) pilot was a MISS. Audio is display-only, and the engine never reads it. The paper adds two concrete cautions. First, a change of channel (microphone or venue) can wipe out feature-level findings. Second, a sample of one sex hides the sex confound in pitch variability. Melange measured that confound, but the fix is not on the live branch (see flags).

They note two different microphones may have contributed to this, alongside noise, colds and fatigue. Voice alone reached about 60 percent best-case three-class accuracy against over 75 percent for facial-expression work, and they call personality prediction multimodal.
